title: Foreign Minister Khanal visits Nepali Consulate General in New York - Khabarhub
description: Foreign Minister Khanal visits Nepali Consulate General in New York  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal visited the Nepali Consulate General in New York, the United States, on Tuesday.

Khanal, who is in New York to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, was briefed on the consulate’s activities, services and matters concerning the Nepali community.

During a briefing hosted by Consul General Dadhiram Bhandari, Khanal was briefed on the role of Nepali diplomatic missions abroad in protecting national interests, providing consular services to Nepali citizens, and strengthening Nepal’s economic, social and cultural ties.

Consulate officials also briefed the minister on ongoing activities, future plans and efforts to improve service delivery.

On the occasion, Khanal called for continued coordination and cooperation among relevant agencies to ensure prompt and effective services to Nepali citizens and to further promote Nepal’s interests abroad.

Students from U.S. universities have expressed profound excitement after receiving a reply letter from Chinese President Xi Jinping, vowing to deepen friendly ties and cultural exchanges with China. Recently, nearly 100 students from Harvard University and nine other U.S. universities wrote to Xi, sharing their experiences and what they had gained from the Future Makers 2026 China-U.S. Youth Tour for a Shared Asia-Pacific Future and other exchange events in China, and expressing their willingness to contribute to promoting China-U.S. friendship.

A reply has arrived, just before Xi's state visit to the United States.

In his letter, Xi welcomed the students' appreciation for Chinese civilization, their hope for friendly cooperation between China and the United States, and their willingness to act as envoys of friendship bridging the Pacific Ocean.

Noting that young people from both countries share the same planet Earth and jointly shoulder the mission of the times, Xi urged them to advance China-U.S. friendly cooperation, foster mutual understanding and affinity between the two peoples, and contribute the vitality of youth to building a better world.

After returning from their trip, students at Central Michigan University agreed that they had come home with a renewed perspective. Now that they had actually set foot in China, what they saw was more concrete than what they had previously learned from the classroom, books, or the internet.

"I've only really learned a lot about China in class through my studies, through books, and actually going there to experience China was completely different. You never really know what a culture is like until you go and experience it yourself. So going there and actually stepping on the ground and talking to people and learning about their lives was just so much more than I could ever have learned in a book," said Kiana Haywood, a senior student at Central Michigan University.

"When I got there, I learned that we were all actually very much more similar than we thought. We found that American and Chinese students were so unbelievably closely related. We found that we have the same humor. We have the same stress. We share so many things in common that we had just not known about," said Kevin Baker, a sophomore at Central Michigan University.

Since President Xi launched an initiative to invite 50,000 young Americans to China for exchange and study programs over a five-year span in November 2023, over 50,000 young Americans have visited China, achieving the target two and a half years ahead of schedule.

The university students recognized that the initiative had helped bring their exchange trip to China into reality, so they wrote to Xi, hoping to express their gratitude and to let the Chinese president know what the experience had meant to them.

"I think doing what we are doing right now and just kind of spreading that message, really emphasizing the importance of programs like these," said Grace, another student from Central Michigan University.

"We wrote a letter because we kind of want to just help him realize like how amazing the experience was that we were able to participate in and just tell him we need more opportunities like these," said Haywood.

Xi's reply encouraged the students to continue seeking exchanges, building on the experience they had through the program. That message resonated deeply with the participants.

"I think the part where he talked about how important it is to continue this exchange, and that made me think about the students that we met and making sure we continue the friendships that we built on this trip because I was the whole point of the trip, really getting to experience each other's culture," said Grace.

Speaking of the meeting between the two heads of state, the American students said they hope it will promote more exchanges between the two countries.

"I think it's going to be a really great opportunity, especially because we can continue talks about a shared future between our two nations, especially because with how the world is, we do really want to have that strong connection to other nations right now," Baker said.

title: Nepal's disaster reflects growing climate crisis: UN Secretary-General - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal's disaster reflects growing climate crisis: UN Secretary-General  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Sept 23: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has drawn the world attention that recent disaster in Nepal had demonstrated the impact of climate crisis.

In the opening of 81st session of UN General Assembly in New York today, Secretary-General Guterres viewed the mountain countries, including Nepal, have suffered most owing to global temperature rise. The world will see further hazards with increasing temperature causing glacier melt, he warned.

The world leader also reminded the warning he had issued from Nepal to the world on fast melting of glaciers. "I'd issued warning three years back that the world roof was caving in," he said, adding that there were some taking the warning as a stretch then. But the present Bhotekoshi flood in Nepal has proved that the climate change impacts are quicker and more serious and more intense than expected.

He further said climate change is not a concern merely for future but it has become a present reality. But the countries having little role in global carbon emission are bearing the brunt, according to him.

Secretary- General Guterres argued the countries responsible for pollution should pay the price and those at the receiving end deserve compensation and financial assistance.

"There is not adequate budget in the dedicated fund for loss and damage. I urge the developed countries to abide by their climate finance commitments," the UN Secretary-General said, asking the world leaders and representatives at the UN General Assembly to increase finance for climate adaptation three fold and mobilize additional resource to the loss and damage fund.(RSS)

title: US announces additional $31 million in aid for Nepal - Khabarhub
description: US announces additional $31 million in aid for Nepal  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: The United States has announced an additional $31 million in assistance to Nepal to support ongoing relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts following the August 26 Bhote Koshi floods.

US Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker announced the assistance during a meeting with Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal in New York on Tuesday.

According to the US Embassy in Nepal, $10 million of the assistance will be allocated for permanent, specially designed bridges to be supplied by US companies. The bridges are expected to restore critical transportation infrastructure in the flood-affected areas and improve regional connectivity.

Hooker also announced an additional $8 million for water, sanitation and hygiene services, as well as shelter, security, livelihoods and winterization assistance for families affected by the floods.

The US Embassy in Nepal will provide another $13 million worth of US-made drones to strengthen Nepal’s capacity to respond to and recover from future disasters, the embassy said.

With the latest commitment, total US assistance for Nepal’s flood response and recovery efforts has surpassed $36 million. The US government said it will continue working closely with the Government of Nepal and provide additional assistance as needed.

title: BREAKING NEWS: Nepal to ban resettlement in flood-hit areas, 33,000 likely affected - Japan Wire by Kyodo News
description: BREAKING NEWS: Nepal to ban resettlement in flood-hit areas, 33,000 likely affected  Japan Wire by Kyodo News
publisher.title: Japan Wire by Kyodo News
full_article:
Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told Kyodo News in an exclusive interview that the areas where flood marks -- in some places 13 meters higher than normal river levels -- are visible are to be declared "danger zones."

"We know there is a possibility of future disaster. So, we don't want to take more risk," Uprety said earlier this week, adding that the affected population, estimated to be around 33,000 people, would be resettled in safer areas.

The Aug. 26 flood and debris flow triggered, according to Nepal's government, by an ice-and-rock avalanche in the upper Lhende Khola watershed in Tibet killed 1,451 people and have left about 5,700 people, including over 600 foreign nationals, missing in Nepal. Of the missing, five are Japanese nationals.

Uprety acknowledged that sentimental attachment to places where people are born and spend their lifetime poses a challenge in convincing flood-affected people to move to a safer place.

But he said teams from his office, the Department of Survey, and relevant ministries have already scouted safer areas close to the danger zones, so that the flood-affected can move to "safe settlement" and live with "dignity."

Search operations at the tunnels of some of the 12 hydropower projects pummeled by the avalanche debris are winding down. Authorities are planning to announce the conclusion of such operations and move to post-disaster recovery at the end of this week.

"There is very, very little chance or no chance of getting any survivor," he said.

The government has decided to extend the immediate assistance of approximately $2,600, or 400,000 Nepalese rupees, to each family as a housing grant, on top of a monthly allowance of $98, or 15,000 Nepalese rupees, to each family of up to four members as livelihood and rental support.

For each additional member to the four-member household, an extra 2,000 rupees is provided as livelihood and rental support.

Earlier this month, the government estimated $4.77 billion would be needed for initial recovery from the flood, but Uprety said the amount is expected to increase.

"That ($4.77 billion) is an initial estimate based on rapid assessment. It did not include the costs the government will have to bear to compensate flood-affected citizens for nationalizing their privately-owned land, now designated as a danger zone," he said.

"The final recovery need could very easily be double the initial estimate," Uprety told Kyodo News.

Cash-strapped Nepal is hoping that part of the need will be met through Nepal's development partners including Japan, China, India, Britain, the World Bank, and the Asian Development Bank, among others.

title: Seven decades of Nepal at the UN: From Chuda Prasad Sharma to KP Oli - The Kathmandu Post
description: Seven decades of Nepal at the UN: From Chuda Prasad Sharma to KP Oli  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The United Nations General Assembly is underway in New York, where Prime Minister Balendra Shah is leading Nepal’s delegation. He is scheduled to address the Assembly on September 24.

Shah’s visit is being closely watched. It is his first foreign trip since becoming prime minister, while his address comes less than a month after devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi corridor intensified calls for climate justice.

Nepal is expected to use the UN platform to highlight the disproportionate impact of climate change on a country that contributes little to global greenhouse gas emissions.

Nepal’s engagement with the General Assembly goes back seven decades. It first took part in the 11th session in 1956, with then foreign minister Chuda Prasad Sharma delivering its first address on November 29.

Since then, Nepal has been represented at the Assembly by kings, presidents, prime ministers, foreign ministers and senior diplomats. Their speeches have reflected the country’s changing political system as well as its long-standing foreign policy concerns, from non-alignment and the interests of small and landlocked states to peacekeeping, development, climate change and reform of the UN system.

What issues has Nepal raised over the decades, and how have its priorities at the world’s largest multilateral forum changed?

Chuda Prasad Sharma’s first address

Nepal joined the United Nations on December 14, 1955, becoming its 76th member. It participated in the 11th General Assembly the following year, with Sharma delivering the country’s first address on November 29, 1956. The UN’s digital records identify Sharma as Nepal’s speaker at the opening of the general debate that year.

Nepal was then emerging from the Rana regime and establishing a new political order. Sharma used the international platform to explain Nepal’s political transition and outline its foreign policy.

Non-alignment was central to the speech. Nepal said it would not commit itself in advance to any power bloc and would judge international questions on their merits. Sharma also spoke against racial discrimination, imperialism and the establishment of military bases in other countries.

The emphasis reflected Nepal’s position as a small state situated between India and China at a time when the Cold War was shaping international politics.

King Mahendra’s case for the UN as a shield for small states

Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala addressed the 15th General Assembly in 1960, while Tulsi Giri spoke at the 18th session in 1963. King Mahendra addressed a special high-level session in 1967.

For Mahendra, the UN was particularly important to countries such as Nepal because it offered small states a platform in an international system dominated by major powers.

His argument was that the organisation could provide both a practical and moral framework for protecting smaller countries from external pressure and interference.

The theme of small-state security would recur in Nepal’s later UN speeches, as successive governments stressed that international rules should apply to countries regardless of their size or military and economic power.

Girija Prasad Koirala puts SAARC and post-Cold War order in focus

Prime Minister Girija Prasad Koirala addressed the 48th General Assembly on October 13, 1993, following the restoration of multiparty democracy.

He highlighted constitutional guarantees of human rights and fundamental freedoms and spoke of efforts to improve people’s living standards. He also stressed Nepal’s relations with its neighbours and its engagement in the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).

The end of the Cold War was another major theme. Koirala argued that the post-Cold War world required stronger international arrangements to promote peace and development.

The following years saw Nepal repeatedly highlight the difficulties faced by least developed and landlocked countries. Prime ministers Sher Bahadur Deuba, Krishna Prasad Bhattarai and Koirala, in their addresses in 1995, 1999 and 2000, respectively, called for greater bilateral and multilateral support for countries facing structural geographical and economic disadvantages.

Nepal also raised UN reform, conflicts in South Asia and the SAARC agenda.

Climate change enters Nepal’s UN agenda

Pushpa Kamal Dahal, the first prime minister of republican Nepal, addressed the 63rd General Assembly on September 26, 2008.

His speech focused on Nepal’s peace process, which followed the 2006 Comprehensive Peace Agreement and the election of the Constituent Assembly. He described the process as an opportunity to transform Nepal into a new federal democratic republic and thanked the UN for its support.

Dahal called for easier access to climate finance to support low-carbon and climate-resilient development. He also urged the international community to implement the loss and damage fund, fulfil the $100 billion climate finance commitment and double adaptation finance.

He highlighted what he described as the injustice facing Nepal, a country with extensive forests and rich biodiversity that contributes little to global greenhouse gas emissions but is highly vulnerable to climate change. Nepal’s high mountains, he said, were particularly exposed to the consequences of a crisis the country had done little to cause.

Dahal warned that melting glaciers and changing weather patterns posed serious risks to Nepal and called for international support to protect the country’s environment. He also linked climate vulnerability with the development challenges facing least developed and landlocked countries.

The issue would become a recurring theme in Nepal’s subsequent UN addresses.

From climate vulnerability to climate justice

Prime Minister Madhav Kumar Nepal, addressing the 64th General Assembly in 2009, continued to highlight climate change. He warned about the risks posed by glacial lake outburst floods and increasingly destructive flash floods while also discussing Nepal’s peace process and transitional justice.

Baburam Bhattarai, addressing the 66th session, Khil Raj Regmi at the 68th and Sushil Koirala at the 69th, continued to raise the concerns of least developed countries, oppose terrorism and highlight the effects of climate change on mountainous countries.

Regmi also raised the issue of climate justice.

Across these speeches, Nepal continued to emphasise the need to complete the peace process and strengthen the country’s democratic transition.

Constitution, climate and the concerns of LDCs

Sher Bahadur Deuba addressed the 72nd General Assembly in 2017, while KP Sharma Oli addressed the 73rd, 75th and 79th sessions. Dahal returned to the rostrum for the 78th session in 2023.

Their speeches covered several recurring themes: implementation of Nepal’s constitution, opposition to terrorism, climate change and the interests of least developed countries.

Deuba argued that Nepal’s low contribution to global emissions contrasted sharply with the severity of the climate impacts it faced, and called for effective implementation of the Paris Agreement. In his 2017 address, he also stressed the importance of small states and their role in the UN system.

Dahal’s 2023 address, delivered as Nepal was chairing the LDC group, again called for greater climate finance and stronger international action. He said mountainous countries such as Nepal were bearing a severe share of the impacts of climate change and called for easier access to climate finance, early implementation of the loss and damage fund and fulfilment of the $100 billion climate finance commitment.

Oli’s emphasis on multilateralism

Oli’s addresses increasingly placed multilateralism at the centre of Nepal’s international message.

In his 2020 address to the 75th General Assembly, delivered during the Covid-19 pandemic, Oli argued that global challenges such as the pandemic, climate change, inequality and insecurity required stronger international cooperation.

He said multilateral cooperation had suffered from unilateral tendencies and protectionist policies and argued that global interests, rather than narrow national interests, should underpin the rules-based international order.

Oli also repeated Nepal’s argument that its mountains were of global significance and that the country, despite making a negligible contribution to greenhouse gas emissions, was bearing a disproportionate share of the consequences. He called for effective implementation of the Paris Agreement and greater access to climate finance.

He also highlighted the need for international solidarity and recalled UN Secretary-General António Guterres’ visit to Nepal the previous year, when Guterres had used his visit to draw attention to both the importance of peace and the climate crisis facing the Himalayas.

That combination of multilateralism and climate vulnerability has become one of the most consistent features of Nepal’s recent UN diplomacy.

What will PM Shah say?

Prime Minister Shah, who left for New York on Tuesday, is expected to highlight the impact of climate change on Nepal and press its case for climate justice.

He will address the 81st General Assembly less than a month after the devastating Bhotekoshi floods, which have renewed calls for greater international support for climate-vulnerable countries.

title: Warming Himalayas: Nepal’s Climate Justice Test - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
description: Warming Himalayas: Nepal’s Climate Justice Test  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
publisher.title: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
full_article:
The recent floods in Nepal exposed the growing vulnerability of Himalayan communities and the widening gap between the scale of climate losses and international support. The devastating Himalayan disaster of August 26, 2026, has left Nepal facing enormous reconstruction costs. The critical question for the global community is whether climate finance will be treated as a matter of justice, instead of charity.

The high-altitude glacier collapse in the northern part of Langtang/Lirung Mountain caused a Himalayan tsunami that killed more than 1,451 people as of September 19, 2026, left 5,786 missing, and affected about 1.6 million people in five districts of Nepal, according to the government’s situation report .

The Nepali government has rescued 13,784 people and mobilized security forces for rescue operations. It assessed damage to 41 motorable bridges, 3,702 private houses, roads, and 12 hydropower projects.

The recently released Rapid Damage and Need Assessment (RDNA) estimates total damage and losses at more than $2.66 billion. About $4.72 billion is required for reconstruction and rehabilitation, while $5.7 million is needed for immediate relief and short-term rehabilitation over the next six months.

The flood damaged 7,570 private houses, 48 public buildings, 18 schools, seven health facilities, and 30 cultural heritage sites. About $685 million will be required to rehabilitate the social sector.

But the cost of physical damage does not capture the full social impact. Children, women, and senior citizens have suffered severe psychosocial impact, while marginalized communities have become further marginalized. These “costs” have been undermined or overlooked in the assessment report.

Scientists working with World Weather Attribution (WWA) described the disaster as a “catastrophic rock-ice avalanche that transitioned into a debris flood in the Himalayas along the Nepal-China border.” They said climate change and rising temperatures in the Himalayan region contributed significantly to the disaster. Floods in the Himalayan region have become more frequent and more devastating in recent years.

The government of Nepal has written to the Loss and Damage Fund , seeking reparation for the impacts of climate change and calling on polluters to provide compensation and justice. The Loss and Damage Fund said Nepal should provide sufficient evidence about the causes of the flood. Its board will consider providing up to $20 million in compensation. Compared with the estimated losses, the proposed support is small.

The World Bank has also offered concessional loans to Nepal. Members of the civil society and youth are demanding grants as reparation rather than loans. They have been demanding climate justice, focusing on the causes of glacier melt in the Himalayas, known as the “Third Pole” and a source of water for large numbers of people in the region.

Campaigners argue that the climate crisis is a fundamental human rights issue linked to the right to life and a sustainable environment. They are also calling for climate finance to be treated as justice rather than charity and for a regional framework across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region to share information, establish early-warning systems and develop institutional mechanisms.

Ten young people began a hunger strike on September 18, 2026, at the base camp of Mount Manaslu. They are demanding assessments of future glacial lake outburst flood risks, regular joint monitoring of lakes along the China-Nepal border, and climate compensation and justice for Nepal, which has to bear the costs of climate-related impacts to which it has not contributed.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah is attending the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, where he will raise the issue of climate crisis impacting Nepal. It is an opportunity for Nepal to present the context and causes of the recent disaster internationally. Foreign Minister Sisir Khanal has already left for the UNGA and is due to attend side events in New York. He is also expected to appeal for international support to overcome the crisis.

Civil society and the public have raised concerns about delays in rescuing people trapped in a hydropower tunnel, saying the government did not allow international experts to assist during the early phase of the rescue. They have also raised concerns about delays in search operations.

Nepal will need to amplify its demands for climate justice, including through the Loss and Damage Fund, while ensuring accountability and transparency in the use of funds. The federal government’s initial hesitation to collaborate with local governments also created tensions between federal and provincial governments.

The internally displaced are being housed in 27 holding centers in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading, where 1,743 people are living. The government has offered $98 (15,000 Nepali rupees) per family member to stay outside the holding centers for four months.

The disaster gives Nepal an opportunity to raise concerns about climate change at the global and regional levels. Communities living in river basins and near glacier lakes remain at high risk. Nepal should seek timely information-sharing from the international community to reduce those risks, while international partners can provide technology for faster warnings.

Existing early-warning technology and knowledge may not be sufficient to predict disasters of this kind. Investment is, therefore, needed not only for recovery but also for research and knowledge exchange. Digital technology and empowered communities could help reduce vulnerabilities.

Nepal also needs people-centered development to cope with such disasters, including the exchange of knowledge on infrastructure capable of withstanding harsh Himalayan conditions. Nepal, China, and India need to minimize human activities that directly or indirectly affect the ecology and environment of the Himalayas.

Community-led initiatives, respect for indigenous knowledge and participation in development could help sustain the region’s ecology and reduce degradation.

Small states such as Nepal need global support to rebuild after large-scale disasters. The Government of Nepal also needs to prioritize community rebuilding in future interventions rather than focusing on the business community.

title: The response to Nepal’s disaster is a test for global climate institutions - Climate Home News
description: The response to Nepal’s disaster is a test for global climate institutions  Climate Home News
publisher.title: Climate Home News
full_article:
Dharam R Uprety is head of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The climate crisis didn’t just knock at our doorstep. It has smashed through homes, demolished critical roads, and caused untold grief for millions of Nepali people. It has now been nearly a month since a wall of ice, rock, and water tore through the Bhote Koshi river system. The death toll has risen to nearly 1,500 people with 5,800 more still missing.

Nepal needs sustained assistance from the international community.

We are staring at a reconstruction bill of at least $5 billion, as we laid out in our letter to the co-chairs of the Board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage on September 1. This constitutes a tenth of our entire economy, and we cannot afford to be saddled with greater loans. We asked the Board to treat the Bhote Koshi disaster as the special case that it is: sudden, unprecedented and exceptional.

The Loss and Damage fund currently holds $820 million in pledges, yet not a single dollar has yet been disbursed for the nearly $3 billion in requests. Its next scheduled meeting is not until December, in Manila. Nepal cannot wait that long, and neither can the next country this happens to.

As loss and damage fund stalls, Nepal crowdfunds flood relief

The tragedy must also serve as a wake up call for immediate climate action. A new study from the World Weather Attribution has found that global warming was a likely contributing factor for the avalanche.

Bandaid solutions are no longer enough; the world needs to transition away from fossil fuels and accelerate investment in clean sources of energy.

Disproportionate impact

The Nepal government has set an ambitious target to replace petrol/diesel vehicles with electric vehicles (EVs) by 2031. The country also already gets most of its electricity from clean sources, with plans for further expansion within the next decade. Our forest cover has grown to 46 percent.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of the planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions. Major polluters need to step up their efforts, so that countries like mine stop bearing a disproportionate impact.

Global emissions are still rising, while countries such as the US, the UK, Australia and several others have drastically reduced the foreign aid that they provide to the rest of the world. And at the same time, they are continuing to increase their fossil fuel production. That is not only unjust, it is also unsustainable for a planet that is already showing us how little room for error remains.

What happened in Bhote Koshi is not unique to the Hindu Kush Himalaya. In May 2025, a nearly identical disaster buried the Swiss village of Blatten, when a rock and ice avalanche tore off the Birch Glacier above it. A study published this month found the avalanche needed almost no friction to travel as far and as fast as it did, a sign of just how destabilised that mountainside had become.

In the Arctic, researchers reported this week that thawing permafrost on the Norwegian island of Jan Mayen turned an ordinary magnitude 6.5 earthquake into the island’s first major glacier rock avalanche in 40 years, the kind of tremor that would once have caused only minor disruption.

From the Alps to the Arctic to the Himalaya, the same warming is loosening the ice and rock that used to hold these mountains together. The next Bhote Koshi could strike anywhere that grip is failing.

Growing focus on mountains in UN climate process

This is not the first time we have tried to get the world’s attention on the mountain ecosystem. At COP30 in Belem last November, Nepal led the push to put mountains on the global climate agenda for the first time, through our Sagarmatha to Belém initiative.

That effort got mountain ecosystems written into the COP30 cover decision and the Global Goal on Adaptation, marking the strongest visibility mountain issues have ever received at the UN climate process. We also secured the first Annual Dialogue on Mountains and Climate Change, which was held at the UN climate talks in June this year at Bonn.

We used COP30 as a platform to warn that retreating glaciers and destabilised mountain systems were not a distant risk. Ten months later, that warning became the Bhote Koshi disaster.

The UN General Assembly and upcoming UN climate talks in Antalya will be two fora for world leaders to show solidarity and more importantly, show how they intend to walk the talk.

Nepal flood destruction shows “limits to adaptation”, scientists say

In the near-term, the Loss and Damage board has been requested to hold an emergency meeting to consider Nepal’s difficult situation. Several nations have generously stepped up to offer physical relief and direct aid. This is greatly welcome. Our needs, unfortunately, far exceed that.

Every impacted village needs a chance to rebuild, children need to see their schools back in operation, and the roads that are the lifeline of communities require urgent reconstruction. Some things may have been lost permanently, but through investment in monitoring and early warning systems, the government of Nepal can try to ensure a future event does not unfold yet another unimaginable tragedy.

This was not just someone else’s disaster that affected the people of Dhading, Rasuwa, and Nuwakot. It is a shared emergency, across Nepal and the world over as more and more communities become victims to a crisis they did not create. This is why, even as we cope with relief and rescue efforts, we are taking the time to present data and share our needs around this climate injustice.

title: PM Shah arrives in New York to lead Nepal’s UN delegation - The Kathmandu Post
description: PM Shah arrives in New York to lead Nepal’s UN delegation  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah arrived in New York on Wednesday to lead Nepal’s delegation to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Shah was received at John F Kennedy International Airport by Nepal’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Lok Bahadur Thapa, along with other Nepali diplomats.

The prime minister is scheduled to pay a courtesy call on UN Secretary-General António Guterres on Wednesday. He will also attend a reception hosted by Nepal’s mission in New York.
